summary.one_line: India's largest and lowest-cost coal producer, debt-free and highly cash-generative. But this is a 100% offer for sale by parent Coal India, so MCL gets no money from it. Revenue, operating margin and profit have fallen two years running, H1 FY27 output fell 9%, prices are administered, and a large state-levy exposure is unresolved. Quality asset, weak growth case: track rather than apply.
bull_points: Largest single coal producer in India: 218.31 MT in FY26, 21.00% of domestic output, with audited JORC reserves of 9,840.31 MT, about 45 years at current output (S2)
Effectively debt-free: borrowings of Rs 3.16 crore against net worth of Rs 21,371 crore at March 2026, with net worth rising every year (S2, S3)
Strong cash generation in FY26: operating cash flow of Rs 12,478 crore against PAT of Rs 10,698 crore, alongside about Rs 8,400 crore of dividends declared (S2, S9)
Nearly all output (99.85%) is opencast and mechanised, and rail carries a rising share of dispatches (65.28% in FY26 vs 58.70% in FY24), which supports its cost position (S2, S6)
H1 FY27 revenue rose 9.3% to Rs 16,093 crore and PAT rose 6.7% to Rs 4,881 crore on higher offtake (S2, S7)
bear_points: 100% offer for sale: Coal India receives all proceeds, and MCL gets no capital for growth (S2, S10)
Revenue fell from Rs 31,634 crore (FY24) to Rs 30,550 crore (FY26), operating EBITDA margin fell from 46.41% to 41.69%, and PAT fell from Rs 11,842 crore to Rs 10,698 crore (S2)
H1 FY27 production fell to 87.54 MT from 96.53 MT and overburden removal fell about 21%. The higher H1 offtake (127% of production) drew down stock rather than coming from new output (S2)
About 82% of sales are under fuel supply agreements at Coal India-notified prices, and the e-auction premium shrank from about Rs 802/t in FY24 to about Rs 275/t in FY26 (S6, S7)
Contingent liabilities equal 55.86% of net worth (Sep 2026). Separately, a mineral-levy exposure of about Rs 31,228 crore, estimated by Coal India's legal department, is not provided for (S2, S7)
watch_points: Whether FY27 production recovers toward the expansion trajectory management has described (285 MT by FY29) after the H1 FY27 decline (S2, S14)
Outcome of state mineral-levy claims and environmental-clearance demand notices (S7)
Trade receivable days rose from 22 (FY24) to 41 (FY26). Watch collection from state utilities (S2)
Further stake sales by Coal India: government approval allows dilution of up to 25%, and only 10% is sold now (S12, S27)
Final subscription by category on 23 November. Day-1 figures were only intraday snapshots (S5)

reasoning: The money does not go to the business. The entire Rs 8,981 crore issue is Coal India selling 10% of its stake, so MCL receives nothing for capex, new mines or diversification. Buyers are funding the parent's monetisation, not MCL's growth (S2, S10).

The asset is excellent but the growth story is not yet visible. MCL is India's largest coal producer with roughly 45 years of reserves and almost no debt. Yet revenue, operating EBITDA and PAT all fell between FY24 and FY26, and H1 FY27 production fell 9.3% year on year (S2, S7).

The moat is real but sits largely with the state. MCL's low-cost opencast geology, Odisha reserves and rail evacuation are hard to copy. But Coal India notifies its prices, and its premium e-auction realisations have collapsed. That limits how much of its cost advantage shareholders can capture (S2, S6).

Governance is controlled by the promoter rather than run by it, and minority interests come second. The Government and Coal India keep 90%, executives are seconded from Coal India on terms it can change, and dividend policy follows CPSE rules. A minority investor rides along with parent priorities, including possible further stake sales of up to 25% in total (S2, S9, S12).

The tail risk is not small. Contingent liabilities equal 55.86% of net worth, about Rs 11,813 crore of litigation is pending against the company, and a roughly Rs 31,228 crore mineral-levy exposure is unprovided. That exposure is close to three years of FY26 profit (S2, S7).

What would change the call to invest: confirmed production recovery in H2 FY27, stabilising realisations and receivable days, and clarity on the levy exposure. All can be checked from post-listing quarterly disclosures, so tracking costs little (S2, S7).

subsections.title: What MCL does and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL) was carved out of South Eastern Coalfields in April 1992 and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Coal India Limited (S11). It mines and sells non-coking (thermal) coal, including some washed or beneficiated coal, from the Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields in Odisha. It is the largest single coal producer in India, at 21.00% of domestic production in FY26 (S2). It sells only in India and reports a single segment, coal mining and related services (S2).

Revenue is almost entirely from raw non-coking coal, which made up 97.41% of product sales in FY26 and 97.38% in H1 FY27 (S2). Pricing has two tracks. About 82.12% of FY26 product sales went through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs) at grade-wise base prices notified centrally by Coal India, averaging roughly Rs 1,354/tonne. The remaining 17.88% was sold through e-auctions at roughly Rs 1,797/tonne (S6). MCL mainly produces lower-heat utility grades (G11 to G14) (S6). It does not set its own price list, which is the most important thing to understand about how it earns money.

blocks.caption: Revenue per tonne dispatched (derived: revenue from operations / dispatch), Rs per tonne

blocks.text: Volumes rose about 6% from FY24 to FY26 while revenue fell. Revenue per tonne dropped about 9% (derived from S2). Per Finshots, the e-auction premium over notified prices narrowed from about Rs 802/t in FY24 to about Rs 275/t in FY26 (S6). This explains the falling-revenue trend.

As of 30 June 2026, MCL ran 17 mines: 14 opencast and 3 underground. It deploys about 70 owned and contracted surface miners and operates one coal washery plus coal handling plants, silos and rapid loading systems (S11). Its Ib Valley washery has an annual capacity of 10 million tonnes (S16). It holds about 33,508.79 hectares of land, including 30,192.14 hectares of mining and surface rights under the Coal Bearing Areas Act (S11). Opencast mining delivered 99.85% of FY26 output (S2).

The supply chain runs from mine to customer through contractors and rail. MCL relies heavily on third-party contractors. Its top 10 contractors took 60.02% of contractual expenses in FY26 and 63.61% in H1 FY27, up from 42.62% in FY24 (S2). On evacuation, rail carried 65.28% of FY26 dispatches, up from 58.70% in FY24, while road carried 30.74%. Over 96% of first-mile-connectivity dispatches go by rail, and five seaports handle about 21.5% of dispatches for coastal power plants (S6). Mine planning and technical support come from the Coal India group, including CMPDI (S17).

In H1 FY27, offtake (111.24 MT) far exceeded production (87.54 MT), and overburden removal fell about 21% year on year (S2). The H1 revenue growth therefore came from selling stock, not from mining more. Lower overburden removal can also constrain future coal exposure.

MCL supplies state and private power utilities, captive power plants and IPPs, plus non-power users such as cement and sponge iron (S2). Thermal power took 68.62% of FY26 product sales (S2). Customers span 16 states (S2). Government-owned power generators and utilities contributed 44.81% of FY26 revenue and 41.68% in H1 FY27. The RHP itself flags that this brings regulatory scrutiny and slower collections (S2).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration (% of revenue from operations)
rows: Thermal power sector (% of product sales)

blocks.text: The concentration is real but typical of a thermal-coal supplier whose buyers are a handful of large power utilities bound by long-term FSAs. The risk is less that a customer leaves, since FSAs and rail logistics make switching costly. It is more that state utilities pay slowly: trade receivable days doubled from 22 in FY24 to 41 in FY26 (S2).

Per the CRISIL report in the RHP, coal supplies about 70% of India's electricity generation (FY26) (S2). India's coal resource base was about 411.53 billion tonnes at 1 April 2026, with Odisha the largest at 106.76 Bt (S2). MCL's own coalfields hold about 106.76 Bt of resources (S2). Its FY26 output equalled about 22.40% of India's non-coking coal production (S11).

items: The Coal Secretary has projected India's coal demand rising to about 1.6 billion tonnes by 2030 from about 1.2 billion tonnes now (S20)
The IEA's forecast is more conservative: about 17% demand growth to about 1,522 Mt by 2030 (S21)
Coal India produces close to 80% of national output. Its production fell in March 2026, with four of eight subsidiaries reporting declines, which shows that supply has recently lagged demand (S22)
Solar tariffs of about Rs 2.5-2.6/kWh, versus Rs 6-10/unit cited for coal-based power, show the long-run transition pressure (S22)

blocks.text: So the market is large and still growing in absolute terms through 2030, but external forecasts differ. The long-term direction depends on how quickly renewables plus storage displace marginal coal generation (S6, S21). MCL's sales growth is therefore a volume story inside a regulated market, not a pricing story.

MCL's competitors are its sister Coal India subsidiaries (SECL, CCL, NCL and others), Singareni, the growing captive and commercial coal blocks opened to private miners by coal-sector reforms, and imported thermal coal (S6). The RHP's listed peer set is Coal India, Bharat Coking Coal, NMDC, PT Bukit Asam and Yancoal Australia (S8). The RHP itself notes that other Coal India subsidiaries also mine coal, which creates potential conflicts of interest within the group (S2).

blocks.caption: FY26 operating EBITDA margin vs RHP peer set (operating performance only, not valuation)

blocks.text: There is a genuine moat on the cost side. It comes from geology and position: thick, shallow seams worked by opencast mining with surface miners (99.85% opencast), a 1.31-1.50 stripping ratio, roughly 45 years of audited reserves, rail-led evacuation and port connectivity (S2, S6). Margins well above the peer set reflect this (S8). Statutory allocation of coal-bearing land to a state miner is also a regulatory barrier that a new entrant cannot easily copy.

The moat protects cost and volume, not price. FSA prices are notified by Coal India, and e-auction premiums depend on market tightness (S6, S7). Private commercial and captive mines are a slow-burning competitive threat to marginal volumes (S6). Calling MCL a price-setter would overstate the moat.

subsections.title: Three-year restated P&L and the growth question

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials (Rs crore; converted from Rs million in the abridged prospectus)

blocks.text: Over FY24-FY26 the RHP's own KPIs show a revenue CAGR of -1.73%, an operating EBITDA CAGR of -6.86% and a PAT CAGR of -4.95% (S2). Total income looks flat only because other income (total income minus revenue) nearly doubled, from about Rs 1,676 crore in FY25 to about Rs 3,350 crore in FY26 (derived from S2, S3). Without that, FY26 EBITDA would have fallen as well. Finology's analysis also flags non-recurring income as a consideration (S18).

H1 FY27 is better: revenue +9.3% and PAT +6.7% year on year (S7). But it came from stock liquidation (offtake 127% of production) while operating margin slipped again to 40.07% (S2). Even Mint's review calls it unclear whether this is a sustained recovery (S7).

The multi-year trend does not support a growth story. Both annual comparisons (FY25 vs FY24 and FY26 vs FY25) show lower revenue, lower operating EBITDA and lower PAT (S2). The case for MCL rests on cash generation and reserves, not on demonstrated growth.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, cash flow and red flags

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs crore)

blocks.text: Leverage is a non-issue: borrowings are a few crore against net worth above Rs 21,000 crore (S2, S3). The cash-flow picture is mixed. In FY24, operating cash flow was only about half of PAT, and FY25 was 0.71x. FY26 and H1 FY27 are well above PAT, helped partly by the stock drawdown (S2). The pattern is lumpy, so an investor should look at multi-year cumulative CFO rather than one year.

Dividends absorb most of the free cash. Declared dividends were about Rs 8,600 crore (FY24), Rs 8,350 crore (FY25) and Rs 8,400 crore (FY26), plus Rs 1,850 crore for H1 FY27 and Rs 3,300 crore more declared from 1 October 2026 to the RHP date, all paid to Coal India before listing (S9). The policy follows the CPSE minimum of the higher of 30% of PAT or 4% of net worth (S9). Capex has fallen from Rs 3,840 crore in FY24 to about Rs 2,930 crore, which sits poorly with production-expansion ambitions (S2).

Red flags: (1) receivable days nearly doubled in two years; (2) contingent liabilities equal 55.86% of net worth at Sep 2026, up from 38.09% a year earlier, and are not provided for (S2); (3) the statutory auditors have included emphasis-of-matter and other-matter paragraphs for FY25, FY26 and both half-years, and the previous auditor did so for FY24 (S2). No debt red flag exists.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key issue terms
rows: 66,18,36,300 equity shares of Rs 2 face value (10% of pre-offer capital)
about Rs 8,981 crore at upper band
Employee and eligible Coal India shareholder quotas
Anchor 18 Nov; open 19 Nov; close 23 Nov; allotment 25 Nov; listing 27 Nov 2026 (tentative)
SBI Capital Markets, Axis Capital, BOB Capital Markets, IDBI Capital, IIFL Capital / KFin Technologies

blocks.text: Sources for the table: offer type, shares, BRLMs, registrar and bid dates come from the abridged prospectus (S2). Price band, size, lot size, employee discount and listing date come from S3 and S13. Post-issue, the promoter holding falls from 100% to 90% (S3). Net of the anchor portion and preferential quotas, Chittorgarh shows retail at 50% of the net offer, with separate employee and Coal India shareholder reservations (S3). Coal India shareholders therefore have a dedicated quota.

Weighted average cost of acquisition for Coal India is Rs 0.26 per share (split-adjusted). No shares changed hands in the past three years (S2). This is a decades-old holding being monetised, not a recent pre-IPO round.

subsections.title: Objects of the issue and who pays

blocks.text: The stated objects are only to carry out the offer for sale and to gain the benefits of listing (visibility, brand, liquidity) (S2). MCL will receive no proceeds. All offer proceeds, net of offer expenses and taxes, go to Coal India (S2). Coal India bears the offer-related costs. Any amounts MCL pays on its behalf are reimbursed, and Coal India bears all costs if the offer fails (S10). No monitoring agency is required (S10).

blocks.caption: Use of the Rs ~8,981 crore raised
rows: Offer for sale proceeds to Coal India

blocks.text: For the investment case, this matters a lot. The IPO adds nothing to MCL's capacity, balance sheet or growth capex. An investor is buying a minority slice of an existing cash flow stream from a parent that keeps control and the dividend-setting power (S2, S10).

The promoters are the President of India, acting through the Ministry of Coal, and Coal India Limited. Coal India was incorporated in 1973 as Coal Mines Authority, renamed in 1975, and is described in the RHP as the largest coal producer in the world (S2). Coal India itself reported FY26 consolidated PAT of Rs 31,070.58 crore, down from Rs 35,449.72 crore (S24). MCL alone contributed about a third of that, which shows how central MCL is to its parent (derived from S2, S24).

blocks.caption: Board and KMP (per abridged prospectus)
rows: Part-time Director, Ministry of Coal nominee

blocks.text: The management are career PSU coal executives rather than founder-entrepreneurs. Their track record is the operating record above. CMD Kaole was already leading the company in mid-2025 media interviews, when he reported FY25 output of 225 MT. Production then slipped to 218 MT in FY26, short of the 239 MT target (S2, S15). The abridged prospectus does not give individual tenures or prior roles, so a fuller track-record assessment was not possible. Executives are seconded from Coal India, and Coal India can change their terms at any time (S2). This board as listed has no independent directors. That is common for CPSEs before listing but weak for minority protection, and investors should check post-listing compliance with the independent-director requirements (S2).

The related-party picture is structural rather than hidden. Coal India controls notified pricing for the FSAs that drive about 82% of sales, runs the e-auction scheme, supplies seconded executives, and through CMPDI provides mine planning (S6, S7, S17). It also receives all IPO proceeds and the entire pre-IPO dividend stream (S9, S10). Sister subsidiaries compete in the same coal market, which the RHP itself flags as a conflict of interest (S2). The RHP states that MCL has no identified group companies (S2). The full RPT note with rupee amounts could not be accessed (see method), so this section cannot quantify inter-company balances.

blocks.caption: Outstanding litigation summary (RHP)
rows: 6 (+1 SEBI/stock-exchange disciplinary action in last 5 FY)

blocks.text: Beyond the table, Mint reports a possible exposure to state mineral levies on mineral-bearing land of Rs 31,228 crore, as estimated by Coal India's legal department. It is not a confirmed demand or a recognised liability. A further Rs 2,864 crore of demand notices allege production beyond environmental clearance limits, which MCL is contesting (S7). The clearance issue has history: in 2018 Odisha issued a demand notice of about Rs 8,297 crore on MCL for production in violation of environmental clearance (S19).

The RPT section is not unusual for a PSU subsidiary. The governance concern is control: pricing, dividends, staffing and further stake sales all sit with the parent and the government. The litigation and levy exposure is large relative to annual profit and is the main governance-adjacent risk (S2, S7).

items: Unprovided levy and contingent exposure: contingent liabilities are 55.86% of net worth (Sep 2026), and the potential state mineral-levy exposure is about Rs 31,228 crore, nearly three times FY26 profit (S2, S7)
Administered pricing and shrinking premiums: about 82% of sales are at Coal India-notified FSA prices, and the e-auction premium fell from about Rs 802/t to about Rs 275/t over FY24-FY26 (S6)
Volume execution: H1 FY27 production fell to 87.54 MT from 96.53 MT and overburden removal fell about 21%. Delays in land acquisition, R&R and environmental clearances can slow new mines (S2, S16)
Parent control and conflicts: Coal India controls strategy, staffing (secondment) and dividends, and its sister subsidiaries compete for the same customers (S2, S7)
Customer and receivables risk: the top 10 customers are 55.94% of revenue, government-owned utilities are 44.81%, and receivable days rose from 22 to 41 (S2)
Contractor dependence: the top 10 contractors account for 63.61% of contract costs in H1 FY27 (S2)
Overhang and energy transition: government approval allows Coal India to sell up to 25%, and renewables plus storage threaten long-run thermal coal demand (S6, S27)
Under-insurance and hazardous operations: the RHP states insurance is not in line with industry standards for a hazardous mining business (S2)

blocks.text: Two of these risks are largely unique to MCL rather than prospectus boilerplate: the size of the unprovided levy and clearance exposure, and the fact that production fell while revenue rose in H1 FY27 (S2, S7). Investors should weight those two most heavily.

Reserves are estimates. Part of the resource and reserve data follows Indian ISP guidelines that the DMT has not audited and that differ from international standards (S2). The 45-year life figure uses JORC-audited reserves, but the larger resource figures should not be taken as bankable.

subsections.title: Risks that matter less than they look

blocks.text: Balance-sheet leverage, refinancing and interest-rate risk are negligible: borrowings are under Rs 3 crore (S2). Customer churn risk is also lower than the concentration numbers suggest, because FSAs and rail links tie power plants to specific coalfields (S6). Liquidity risk is low, with a current ratio of about 2x (S2).

The litigation counts look alarming (49 criminal cases against the company). For a 20,000-employee miner with large land holdings they are not unusual. The rupee amounts matter more than the counts (S2).

The RHP strategy section commits to expanding existing mines and developing new ones, coal beneficiation to widen the customer base, evacuation upgrades (first-mile connectivity, silos and rapid loading, rail corridors), mechanisation and digitisation, and diversification into coal gasification, renewables, other minerals and rare earths (S2). These are statements of direction, not quantified guidance.

items: CMD Uday Kaole (July 2025): MCL expects 285 MT by FY29 and 358 MT by FY35, keeping a 28-29% share of Coal India output. He said MCL prepares to deliver 1.5 times its target (S14)

CMD (June 2025): two new Talcher mines with combined reserves of 35 MT, Subhadra and Balabhadra, with Balabhadra targeted for FY30. Output to reach 300 MT by FY30, and about Rs 17,900 crore planned for renewable projects (S15)
Bhubaneswari OCP's FY27 target was raised to 28 MT after producing 26.48 MT in FY26 (S26)
Earlier diversification: MCL sought approval in 2023 for a Rs 34,072 crore greenfield aluminium complex in Odisha (S23). Its current status is not confirmed in the RHP summary

blocks.text: Management's targets are dated mid-2025 and have not been met so far. FY26 production was 218.31 MT against a 239 MT target, and H1 FY27 output fell 9% (S2, S15). FY24-FY26 capex was flat to down (S2). There is no recent, quantified guidance from an investor call, so treat the 285-300 MT targets as aspirations.

Demand-side tailwinds are plausible: national coal demand is projected at 1.5-1.6 billion tonnes by 2030 (S20, S21). MCL has the reserves and evacuation to capture volume (S2). But realisation per tonne has been falling (derived from S2), and the IPO brings no new money for expansion (S10). Growth must therefore be funded from internal accruals after a dividend payout governed by CPSE norms (S9).

The realistic base case is a cash-rich, low-growth utility-like miner. Volume growth may come in low single digits if new mines start on time, and earnings will be sensitive to e-auction premiums and any levy outcome. That is an inference from the RHP data, not management guidance (S2, S7).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 subscription and grey market

blocks.text: Anchor bidding on 18 November raised Rs 2,295 crore by allotting 16,87,68,255 shares at Rs 136, the top of the band (S4). LIC took about Rs 568 crore and Nippon Life India about Rs 500 crore across two schemes. Other anchors included ICICI Prudential, HDFC, Aditya Birla Sun Life, Axis, Motilal Oswal, Edelweiss, GIC Re, Tata, Bajaj Life, SBI General, Tata AIG, Invesco and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (S4). Domestic mutual funds took 53% via 11 fund houses (S4, S3). Zerodha lists tentative anchor lock-in ends of 24 December 2026 and 22 February 2027 (S25).

blocks.caption: Day-1 subscription (partial, intraday as of ~10:20 am IST, 19 Nov 2026)

blocks.text: These are early-morning, first-day figures from a Business Standard live blog (S5). The issue is open until 23 November, and they say nothing yet about final demand. QIB money typically arrives on the last day.

Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated): Investorgain showed about Rs 3.1 on the morning of 19 November (S4). IPO Guru reported a fall from Rs 25 on 13 November to about Rs 7 by 16 November (S28). The GMP is small and falling, but it is not an investment signal and played no part in this report's verdict.

method: Primary source: the SEBI-hosted Abridged Prospectus of the RHP dated 13 Nov 2026 (S2), reached from SEBI's RHP filing page (S1) and read page by page. It supplied the restated financials (FY24-FY26 and both half-years), all KPIs, customer and contractor concentration, risk factors, board/KMP, the litigation summary and the offer structure. All rupee figures were converted from Rs million to Rs crore (divide by 10). Revenue per tonne, other income (total income minus revenue), CFO/PAT and the contingent-liability context are my own derivations from S2/S3 and are labelled as such. MATERIAL GAP: the full RHP/DRHP (500+ pages) was not fetched. The SEBI page carried only the abridged prospectus, and the company IR page, NSE/BSE copies and some review sites returned 403 or no link. Items that come only from the full RHP were therefore cross-checked against secondary RHP-based coverage, using at least two sources where possible: FSA/e-auction mix and realisations (S6, S7), dividend history (S9, partly corroborated by S2 financing outflows), offer-expense arrangements (S10), the mineral-levy and environmental-clearance exposures (S7, single source; the Rs 31,228 crore figure also appeared in search snippets), and peer margins (S8). The detailed related-party transactions note with rupee amounts could NOT be obtained, so the RPT discussion is qualitative and limited to the structural relationships the abridged prospectus and coverage disclose. Management outlook comes from 2025 media interviews (S14, S15); no 2026 investor call was found. Day-1 subscription figures are a single intraday snapshot (S5); end-of-day data was not yet available when this was written on 19 Nov 2026. Some sources marked 'search-result snippet' were seen only in WebSearch results. Where their publication date was not visible, the date field shows the access date (2026-11-19). Valuation metrics (P/E, EV/EBITDA, market cap multiples, peer multiples, GMP-implied valuation) were deliberately excluded. EPS/RoNW figures in the prospectus were not used in the investment reasoning. GMP is reported as unofficial and was not used in the verdict.
